doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Teaching at Manhattan School of Music moves to Zoom
summary: He took a teaching job last September; lessons went to Zoom in March, with audio problems fixed with John Clayton's tips.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: What happened with your teaching? Did you have to go online with private students and so forth?

So I do teach at the Manhattan School of Music, and I’ve always not wanted to be — to take a teaching position, I just always wanted to play. It’s unfortunate, I always have a ton of gigs that I play, and it just happened that last September their professor at the last minute got a better gig and they said, “Hey we’ve got a space we need to fill,” and they’ve been asking me for years, “could you come out — we’ll limit the amount of students, it won’t be hard.” So I taught through the first semester and I was supposed to teach the second semester — right in the middle of March they said, “We’re all done, school is closing, you need to teach your lessons via Zoom.” I’d never heard of Zoom. And I thought I was going to have to have somebody walk me through it. If it’s easy I can

do computer stuff, and then thankfully I have daughters that know that stuff. They’re in their twenties, and so they showed me the light, but it wasn’t a hard thing to learn. So my teaching all went online. It was not a fun thing to do because I felt I was ripping people off. I need to have that one-on-one contact with them. I need to hear your sound. I need to hear your attack.
Right. Not through the airwaves and whatever Zoom —

I worked with John Clayton, the great bassist, and he told me some things to do to tweak the settings on Zoom. He said, “Get a mic, a separate mic, your computer mic isn’t adequate.” And all the teachers kind of got together and sort of helped each other and coached each other as to what they need. But literally, when you play a trumpet towards your computer it tries to, I forget what they call it, balance it. Compress it. So I’d be — when I first started my Zoom lessons like [scats] and it would just get this thing and it would go down and then you couldn’t hear anything. It’s trying to control that sound. And so we worked through that stuff, but that’s been the challenge too, the teaching online.
